Durham
DUR-um
n. (the northern English prince-bishopric built around the shrine of Cuthbert, holding the bones of Bede and the Lindisfarne Gospels)
From Old English dun, a hill, and Old Norse holmr, an island, for the rock in the loop of the Wear.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Durham was founded in 995 when the community of Lindisfarne, driven inland by Viking raids and wandering for a century with the body of Cuthbert, settled on the rock in the loop of the Wear. The cathedral was begun in 1093 and is the finest Norman building in England; its bishops held the office of prince-bishop with regalian powers over the county palatine until 1836, raising armies against the Scots. The relics of Bede were brought here in the eleventh century, and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made in the community that founded it. Durham produced John Cosin, bishop after the Restoration, and had earlier been the see of Cuthbert Tunstall, who refused the Edwardian reforms and was deprived. The dictionary records Durham for the hundred years of wandering. A congregation carrying the body of its dead bishop from place to place for three generations, keeping its books and its daily office, is the church in its most reduced form and the dictionary thinks it instructive.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a shrine as a case for sacred things; palatine as possessing royal privileges; a see as the seat of a bishop; perseverance as continuance in a state of grace; and office as a form of divine service.

expand to see more

SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for depositing sacred things; a sacred place; an altar.

PALATINE, a. Pertaining to a palace; possessing royal privileges; as a county palatine.

SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.

PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; in theology, continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory.

OFFICE, n. In liturgics, a formulary of devotion; the daily service of the church.

Key Scripture

Heb 13:7 — "Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation."

2Ti 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

Heb 12:1 — "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,"

Rev 14:13 — "And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them."

Modern Corruption

Northern English prince-bishopric founded in 995 by the wandering community of Lindisfarne, holding the shrine of Cuthbert and the bones of Bede.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the shrine, which is where the dictionary must be careful, because the thing the Lindisfarne community actually did was faithful and the thing it became was not. Carrying a bishop's body with them was an act of love for a man and for a rule of life; enshrining it for pilgrims to pay at is another matter. Scripture directs the right use of a dead teacher, and it is imitation of his faith rather than attendance at his tomb: “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The honour Scripture pays a finished ministry is to its course and its keeping, “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7); the dead are described as resting from labours that follow them rather than as dispensing favours, “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord” (Rev 14:13); and the living are pictured running inside a crowd of such witnesses, “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1). A cloud of witnesses is a congregation to be imitated. It is not a reliquary.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek mimeomai, to imitate, from mimetes (G3402); Greek dromos (G1408), a course; Greek nephos (G3509), a cloud.

expand to see more

Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, to rule, to go before; “Remember them which have the rule over you”, Hebrews 13:7.

Greek mimetes (G3402) — an imitator, a follower; “whose faith follow”, Hebrews 13:7.

Greek dromos (G1408) — a race, a course; “I have finished my course”, 2 Timothy 4:7.

Greek nephos (G3509) — a cloud, a dense mass; “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses”, Hebrews 12:1.

Greek makarios (G3107) — blessed, happy; “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord”, Revelation 14:13.

Usage

"“whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7) — the right use of a dead teacher."

"“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7) — the honour Scripture pays a ministry."

"“Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord” (Rev 14:13) — the dead rest; they do not dispense."
